Odours
ō´derz
n. pl. (sweet smells, spices, incense; rendering Hebrew nichoach and besem, Greek thumiama and osme)
Latin odor, a smell. In Leviticus the sweet odour is the savour of rest that rises from an accepted sacrifice; in Revelation the odours are the prayers of saints.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The elders before the Lamb have “golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints” (Rev 5:8). Under judgment God says, “I will not smell the savour of your sweet odours” (Lev 26:31). Nebuchadnezzar “commanded that they should offer an oblation and sweet odours” to Daniel (Dan 2:46). Asa was buried in a bed “filled with sweet odours and divers kinds of spices” (2Ch 16:14), and Zedekiah was promised burial “with the burnings of thy fathers… so shall they burn odours for thee” (Jer 34:5). Esther's maids were purified “with sweet odours” (Est 2:12). Paul calls the Philippians' gift “an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable” (Php 4:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines odor as smell, scent; fragrance, sweet scent; and, in the plural, perfumes.

expand to see more

ODOR, n. Smell; scent; fragrance; a sweet or an offensive smell; perfume.

Key Scripture

Rev 5:8 — "And when he had taken the book, the four beasts and four and twenty elders fell down before the Lamb, having every one of them harps, and golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints."

Lev 26:31 — "And I will make your cities waste, and bring your sanctuaries unto desolation, and I will not smell the savour of your sweet odours."

Php 4:18 — "But I have all, and abound: I am full, having received of Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God."

Dan 2:46 — "Then the king Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face, and worshipped Daniel, and commanded that they should offer an oblation and sweet odours unto him."

2Ch 16:14 — "And they buried him in his own sepulchres, which he had made for himself in the city of David, and laid him in the bed which was filled with sweet odours and divers kinds of spices prepared by the apothecaries' art: and they made a very great burning for him."

Modern Corruption

Revelation 5:8 is cited for incense in worship, and the verse says what the odours are.

expand to see more

The golden vials full of odours are the proof-text for the censer in Christian worship, and the text interprets itself in the same clause: which are the prayers of saints. The odours are not something burned in heaven; they are what the saints on earth have said on their knees, arriving before the Lamb as fragrance. To burn incense in the assembly on the strength of this verse is to keep the symbol and lose the thing symbolised, which is the history of every ceremony. Leviticus 26:31 shows the other end of the same truth: sweet odours God will not smell, because the people offering them are in rebellion, and the savour of an offering was never in the smoke. Paul's use is the right one — a gift of money to a prisoner, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable — the fragrance being obedience and love, which is the only incense the New Testament knows.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nichoach (H5207), a soothing savour, rest; besem (H1314), spice, sweet odour; Greek thumiama (G2368), incense; osme (G3744), a smell, fragrance.

expand to see more

Hebrew nichoach (H5207) — sweet savour, rest; Leviticus 26:31, Genesis 8:21; Aramaic nichoach (H5208), Daniel 2:46.

Hebrew besem (H1314) — spice, sweet odour; 2 Chronicles 16:14, Esther 2:12.

Greek thumiama (G2368) — incense, odours; Revelation 5:8, 8:3–4, 18:13; osme (G3744), Philippians 4:18, 2 Corinthians 2:14–16.

Usage

"“Golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints” — the verse interprets itself."

"“I will not smell the savour of your sweet odours” — the savour was never in the smoke."

"“An odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable” — a gift to a prisoner."
